new_statements.relation_note: Catalog has Kanuri with an empty rule. Koelle supplies the earliest description: a per-word marked 'accent' with no positional rule, plus morphological accent on negative-mood finals and the interrogative suffix. Read against Hutchison and Gombe (tone language), Koelle's accent is tone, so this does not support a stress rule.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Koelle marks one 'accented syllable' per word with an acute accent, word by word, and gives no general placement rule; the position varies (ába, kámu, meiro, ngó, ngála, mbéli). He notes accent falls on the second vowel of a diphthong, that syllabic nasals can carry the word accent, that the negative mood always carries a strong accent on its last syllable (making the word 'doubly accented'), and that the interrogative suffix takes a strong accent after several unaccented syllables but is otherwise 'toneless'. In modern terms Koelle's 'accent' is almost certainly his rendering of (high) tone, so this is pre-tonal notation rather than a stress rule.
new_statements.secondary_stress: 'Doubly accented' words in the negative mood (p. 85): a second strong accent on the final syllable in addition to the lexical accent.
new_statements.exceptions: Preface p. viii: informant 'a little uncertain' about 'the quantity of the vowels and the accent'; syllabic nasals (n, ng, m before g, d, b) may take the word accent (p. 11, §8).
new_statements.identity_note: Hutchison describes the Yerwa (Maiduguri, Borno State) dialect and notes Fadawu/Ngumatiwu dialects differ in tone; Koelle's 1854 data come from a Bornu Kanuri speaker (interpreter in Sierra Leone); Trommer's title concerns Kanuri polar tone (variety unknown, not opened); Lukas 1937 is the standard Bornu Kanuri grammar (not opened).

readall_conflicts: Neither assigned work could be opened (Lukas 1937 is lending-restricted on archive.org with search-inside disabled; the Trommer PDF server was unreachable), so no conflict arises from them. Among the on-disk supplementary sources, Koelle (1854) writes a single per-word 'accent' with an acute and never states a placement rule, while Hutchison (Yerwa Kanuri) and Muhammad-Gombe (citing Bulakarima & Shettima 2012) describe Kanuri as a tone language (H/L/falling; five tones incl. rising and mid). This is a difference of analysis, not of data: Koelle's 1854 'accent' is his pre-tonal notation for high tone (he himself calls an unaccented suffix 'toneless' and speaks of interrogation 'expressed by the tone only'). No opened source claims a word-stress rule for Kanuri.

audit.reasoning: The record rests on the standard 363-pp reference grammar of Yerwa Kanuri (Hutchison 1981), which we hold as a full scanned text; the deciding quotation and the domain quotation are both present verbatim at the stated chapters/pages, and a whole-grammar a full-text search for stress/accent by the original readers (re-checked here at the cited lines) shows 'stress' used only for phrase-level emphasis and explicitly denied as the marker of compounding. Glottolog lists nothing later and weightier on phonology; web search turned up no instrumental/prosody study and no competing stress analysis, and the two open items downloaded today (Hutchison's ALMA introduction; Gombe 2019 citing Bulakarima & Shettima 2012) both restate Kanuri as a tone language with H/L plus contour (and mid) tones. sources.quote: Pre-tonal 19th-century description from one displaced speaker in Sierra Leone: 'The accented syllable is indicated by the acute accent'; diphthongs 'when they receive the accent, it is always placed on the last of the two vowels'; syllabic nasals may be 'even assuming the accent of the word'. Koelle himself flags his informant as 'a little uncertain' on 'the quantity of the vowels and the accent'. No tone analysis; superseded by Lukas 1937 and Hutchison 1981, so it does not bear on the tonal coding.
